The Splitting Lemma in any Characteristic

Gert-Martin Greuel    Gerhard Pfister

Abstract

We give a simple proof of the splitting lemma in singularity theory, also known as generalized Morse lemma, for formal power series over arbitrary fields. Our proof for the uniqueness of the residual part in any characteristic is new and was previously unknown in characteristic two. Beyond the formal case, we give proofs for algebraic power series and for convergent real and complex analytic power series, which are new for non-isolated singularities.

1 Introduction

The splitting lemma is of great importance for the classification of singularities. It says that a power series ff splits (up to a coordinate change) as the sum of a quadratic part f(2)f^{(2)} plus a series gg of order at least three, where f(2)f^{(2)} and gg depend on disjoint sets of variables. Moreover, the series gg, the ”residual part”, is unique up to a change of coordinates. The splitting lemma is well kown for power series or differentiable functions ff of order at least two over the real or complex numbers. This result, for differentiable functions, is due to René Thom, who used it for his classification of the 7 elementary catastrophes (see his book [Th75], § 5.2D). Since then it has become an indispensable tool in singularity theory, in particular for the classification of singularities. Thom’s proof, especially for the uniqueness of the residual part, is fairly long and complicated and depends on a determinacy theorem of Tougeron. A proof for convergent power series over the complex numbers can be found in [GLS07] and [dJP00]. A proof for the existence of the splitting for formal power series over algebraically closed fields of positive characteristic is sketched in [GK90].

In this note we give a very simple proof of the splitting lemma (existence and uniqueness of the residual part) for formal power series over an arbitrary field. To prove the uniqueness of the residual part we use only the implicit function theorem and some tricky substitutions, in particular in characteristic two.

The existing of a splitting beyond the formal case is more involved and requires different methods. We prove it for algebraic power series over a real valued field (using the nested Artin approximation theorem) and for convergent complex and real analytic power series (using the existence of a versal unfolding).

We like to emphasize that we do not assume that the power series has an isolated singularity, as it was supposed in the classical complex analytic case.

In order to treat convergent and formal power series at the same time, let KK be a field of arbitrary characteristic together with a real vauation ||:K→ℝ≥0|\ |:K\to{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}11 1 This means |a|=0⇔a=0|a|=0\Leftrightarrow a=0, |a|​|b|=|a​b||a||b|=|ab|, and |a+b|≤|a|+|b||a+b|\leq|a|+|b|.. KK is then called a real valued field. If KK is complete w.r.t. |⁣||\ | (every Cauchy sequence with respect to |⁣||\ | converges in KK) KK is called a complete real valued field. KK is called quasi-complete if the completion K¯\bar{K} of KK is a separable field extension of KK. Note that in characteristic 0 every real valued field is already quasi-complete.

Examples of a complete real valued field are ℂ{\mathbb{C}} resp. ℝ{\mathbb{R}} with the usual absolute value as valuation or any field KK with the trivial valuation (|0|=0,|a|=1|0|=0,|a|=1 if a≠0a\neq 0). Finite fields permit only the trivial valuation. The absolute value on the field of rational numbers makes ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} real valued field, which is not complete. Another example is given by the field of pp-adic numbers. Let pp be a prime number, then the map

We recall some elementary facts about quadratic forms. Two quadratic forms q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} are equivalent (q1∼q2q_{1}\sim q_{2}) if there exists a linear automorphism (a linear change of coordinates) φ\varphi of K⁡[𝒙]K[\boldsymbol{x}] such that q2=φ⁡(q1)q_{2}=\varphi(q_{1}). φ\varphi is defined by the linear forms φ⁡(xi)=φi​(x1,…,xn)\varphi(x_{i})=\varphi_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{n}), i=1,…,ni=1,...,n, and then we have φ⁡(q)=∑ai​j​φi​φj\varphi(q)=\sum a_{ij}\varphi_{i}\varphi_{j}. It follows that the rank of the coefficient matrix AA is independent of the chosen basis and therefore an invariant of the quadratic form qq.

If char(K)≠2(K)\neq 2, one may replace the coefficient matrix AA by the symmetric matrix 12​(A+AT)\frac{1}{2}(A+A^{T}) with the same quadratic form. Therefore one usually assumes in characteristic ≠2\neq 2 that AA is symmetric, that is, ai​j=aj​ia_{ij}=a_{ji}. This is however not possible if char(K)=2(K)=2, and the classification of quadratic forms differs substantially from that in characteristic ≠2\neq 2.

For the proof of the splitting lemma for convergent power series we use the following version of the implicit function theorem and the Artin approximation theorems, where the assumptions on the field KK differ slightly.

Theorem 1.1 (Implicit Function Theorem for Convergent Power Series).

Let KK be a field with a real valuation. Let x=x1,…,xnx=x_{1},\ldots,x_{n} and y=y1,…,ymy=y_{1},\ldots,y_{m} and f=(f1,…,fk)∈K​⟨x,y⟩mf=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{k})\in K\langle x,y\rangle^{m} such that

f⁡(0,0)=0​ and ​det(∂fi∂yj​(0,0))i,j=1,…,m≠0.f(0,0)=0\text{ and }\det\big(\frac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial y_{j}}(0,0)\big)_{i,j=1,...,m}\neq 0.

Then there exists y⁡(x)∈K​⟨x⟩my(x)\in K\langle x\rangle^{m} such that

f⁡(x,y⁡(x))=0​ and ​y​(0)=0.f(x,y(x))=0\text{ and }y(0)=0.

A proof of the theorem is given [N62][Theorem 45.3].

Remark 1.2.

In [N62, Theorem 45.3] Nagata proves the Weierstraß preparation theorem (WPT) without the completeness assumption, from which the implicit function theorem is easily deduced. Proofs of the WPT for complete real valued fields are given at several places (e.g. [KPR75, Satz 2.1.4] or [GLS07, Theorem 1.6]). That the completeness assumption for the WPT (as well as for the Weierstraß division theorem and the Weierstraß finiteness theorem) is not necessary, can also be seen as follows: Let KK be not complete and K¯\bar{K} the completion of KK. In loc. cit. the authors show first that the unit uu and the Weierstraß polynomial pp that appear in WPT exist as formal power series over KK. Then, considering uu and pp as elements of K¯​[[𝐱]]\bar{K}[[\boldsymbol{x}]], they show by estimates that ‖u‖𝛆<∞\|u\|_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}<\infty and ‖p‖𝛆<∞\|p\|_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}<\infty. But since the coefficients of uu and pp are in KK, it follows that u,p∈K​⟨𝐱⟩u,p\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle.

We will use the following approximation theorems.

Theorem 1.3 (Artin Approximation).

Let KK be a real valued field. If the characteristic of KK is positive, we assume additionally that KK is quasi-complete. Let x=x1,…,xnx=x_{1},\ldots,x_{n} and y=y1,…,ymy=y_{1},\ldots,y_{m} and f=(f1,…,fk)∈K​⟨x,y⟩kf=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{k})\in K\langle x,y\rangle^{k}. Let y¯​(x)∈K​[[x]]m\bar{y}(x)\in K[[x]]^{m} be a formal solution of f=0f=0:

f​(x,y¯​(x))=0.f(x,\bar{y}(x))=0.

Then there exists for any integer c>0c>0 a convergent solution yc​(x)∈K​⟨x⟩my_{c}(x)\in K\langle x\rangle^{m}:

f​(x,yc​(x))=0f(x,y_{c}(x))=0

such that

y¯​(x)≡yc​(x)​ mod ​⟨x⟩c.\bar{y}(x)\equiv y_{c}(x)\text{ mod }\langle x\rangle^{c}.

The Theorem was proved in characteristic 00 by M. Artin [A68], in characteristic p>0p>0 for complete valued fields by M. André [A75] and for quasi-complete fields by K.-P. Schemmel [S82].33 3 Schemmel proved that the property of KK being quasi-complete is necessary and sufficient for the Approximation Theorem to be true.

For any field KK let K​⟨𝒙⟩a​l​g⊂K⁡[[𝒙]]K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle^{alg}\subset K[[\boldsymbol{x}]], 𝒙=(x1,…,xn)\boldsymbol{x}=(x_{1},...,x_{n}), denote the ring of algebraic power series.44 4 An algebraic power series is a formal power series f⁡(𝒙)f(\boldsymbol{x}) for which a non-zero polynomial P⁡(𝒙,t)P(\boldsymbol{x},t) exists, such that P⁡(x,f⁡(x))=0P(x,f(x))=0 holds.

Lemma 1.4.

If KK is a real valued field, then K​⟨𝐱⟩a​l​g⊂K​⟨𝐱⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle^{alg}\subset K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle.

Proof.

This can easily be seen using Theorem 1.3 as follows. Assume first that KK is complete. Let f∈K⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩=:S⊂K⁡[[x1,…,xn]]f\in K\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle=:S\subset K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]] be an algebraic power series and F∈S⁡[y]F\in S[y] a polynomial such that F⁡(f)=0.F(f)=0. Theorem 1.3 implies that for every c>0c>0 there exists fc∈Sf_{c}\in S such that F⁡(fc)=0F(f_{c})=0 and f≡fc​ mod ​𝔪cf\equiv f_{c}\text{ mod }\mathfrak{m}^{c}. Since F has only finitely many zeros we have f=fcf=f_{c} for some cc (this follows from the Weierstraß division theorem, [GLS07, Theorem I.1.8]). If KK is not complete we can pass to its completion K¯\bar{K} and obtain that f∈K¯​⟨x1,…​xn⟩∩K⁡[[x1,…,xn]]=K⁡⟨x1,…​xn⟩f\in\bar{K}\langle x_{1},\ldots x_{n}\rangle\cap K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]]=K\langle x_{1},\ldots x_{n}\rangle. ∎

We apply now Artin’s approximation theorem to formulate some results that are of interest in its own (and that are used below) for arbitrary K​⟨𝒙⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle. For a non-negative integer kk we call ff right kk-determined, if for any g∈K​⟨𝒙⟩g\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle with f−g∈𝔪k+1f-g\in\mathfrak{m}^{k+1}, we have f∼rff\sim_{r}f. Moreover, we call

Let KK be a real valued field and quasi-complete if char(K)>0(K)>0. Let f∈𝔪2⊂K​⟨𝐱⟩f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}\subset K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle. If μ⁡(f)<∞\mu(f)<\infty, then ff is right (2​μ​(f)−ord⁡(f)+2)(2\mu(f)-\ord(f)+2)-determined.

2 Splitting Lemma in Characteristic ≠2\neq 2

In this section let KK be a field of characteristic different from 2.

The classification of quadratic forms in characteristic ≠2\neq 2 is classically known (cf. [Wi36, Satz 2]): every quadratic form ff is equivalent to a ”diagonal” form,

f∼a1​x12+…+an​xn2,ai∈K.f\sim a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+...+a_{n}x_{n}^{2},\ a_{i}\in K.

If kk is the rank of H⁡(f)H(f), then f∼a1​x12+…+ak​xk2f\sim a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+...+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}, with ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0 for i=1,…,ki=1,...,k.

Of course, if KK is algebraically closed or, more generally, if ai∈K\sqrt{a_{i}}\in K, then f∼x12+…+xk2f\sim x_{1}^{2}+...+x_{k}^{2}. Moreover, for K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}} we have f∼x12+…+xn02−xn0+12−…−xn0+n12f\sim x_{1}^{2}+...+x_{n_{0}}^{2}-x_{n_{0}+1}^{2}-...-x_{n_{0}+n_{1}}^{2}, k=n0+n1k=n_{0}+n_{1}, (by Jacobi-Sylvester), where (n−k,n0,n1)(n-k,n_{0},n_{1}), the signature of ff, is an invariant of ff. In fact, any classification of quadratic forms for special fields can replace the quadratic part in the splitting lemma below.

We formulate now the splitting lemma as we prove it in this note. While the uniqueness of the residual part holds in general, for the existence we have to distinguish several cases.

Theorem 2.1 (Formal splitting lemma in characteristic ≠2\neq 2).

Let KK be a real valued field.

  1. 1.

    Let f0,f1∈𝔪2⊂K⁡⟨𝒙⟩f_{0},f_{1}\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}\subset K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle and assume that

    f0=a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g0​(xk+1,…,xn)​∼rf1=a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g1​(xk+1,…,xn)f_{0}=a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g_{0}(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n})\rsim f_{1}=a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g_{1}(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n})

    with ai∈K,ai≠0a_{i}\in K,a_{i}\neq 0 and g0,g1∈𝔪3g_{0},g_{1}\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}. Then g0​∼rg1g_{0}\rsim g_{1} in K⁡⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩K\langle x_{k+1},...,x_{n}\rangle.

  2. 2.

    Let f∈K⁡[[𝒙]]f\in K[[\boldsymbol{x}]] and rank⁡H⁡(f)=k\rank H(f)=k. Then

    f​∼ra1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g⁡(xk+1,…,xn)f\ \rsim\ a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n})

    with ai∈K,ai≠0a_{i}\in K,a_{i}\neq 0, and g∈𝔪3g\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}. gg is called the residual part of ff. By 1. it is uniquely determined up to right equivalence in K⁡[[xk+1,…,xn]]K[[x_{k+1},...,x_{n}]].

    The same statement holds if f∈K​⟨𝒙⟩f\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle has an isolated singularity 66 6 We say that f∈K​⟨𝒙⟩f\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle has an isolated singularity if its Milnor number is finite., with g∈K⁡⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩g\in K\langle x_{k+1},...,x_{n}\rangle unique up to right equivalence in K⁡⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩K\langle x_{k+1},...,x_{n}\rangle.

We note that (F1,…,Fk,φk+1,…,φn)(F_{1},...,F_{k},\varphi_{k+1},...,\varphi_{n}) is an automorphism of K⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩K\langle x_{1},...,x_{n}\rangle since (φ1,…,φn)(\varphi_{1},...,\varphi_{n}) is an automorphism and since lil_{i} is the linear part of φi\varphi_{i}. It follows that

To show the existence of ψ\psi, we want to apply the implicit function theorem (Theorem 1.1) to F1,…,FkF_{1},...,F_{k}. For this we must show det(∂Fi∂xj​(0))i,j=1,…,k=det(∂li∂xj)i,j=1,…,k≠0\det\big(\frac{\partial F_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}(0)\big)_{i,j=1,...,k}=\det\big(\frac{\partial l_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\big)_{i,j=1,...,k}\neq 0. 2. As the coefficient matrix of the 2-jet of ff has rank kk, the 22-jet of ff can be transformed into a1​x12+…+ak​xk2a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2} by a linear change of coordinates, as follows from the classification of quadratic forms mentioned above. Hence, we can assume that f⁡(𝒙)=a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g⁡(x1,…,xn)f(\boldsymbol{x})=a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}), g∈𝔪3g\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}.

We prove the existence of the splitting for formal power series by constructing coordinate changes of increasing order, providing a splitting modulo increasing powers of 𝔪\mathfrak{m}, which converge formally to a formal coordinate change. To do so write ff as

f⁡(𝒙)=a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+f3​(xk+1,…,xn)+∑i=1kxi⋅gi​(x1,…,xn),f(\boldsymbol{x})=a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+f_{3}(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n})+\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i}\cdot g_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\,,

with ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0, gi∈𝔪2g_{i}\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}, and f3∈𝔪3f_{3}\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}. The coordinate change xi↦xi−12​ai​gix_{i}\mapsto x_{i}-\frac{1}{2a_{i}}g_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k, and xi↦xix_{i}\mapsto x_{i} for i>ki>k, yields

with hi∈𝔪3h_{i}\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}, f4∈𝔪4f_{4}\in\mathfrak{m}^{4}. Continuing with hih_{i} instead of gig_{i} in the same manner, the last sum will be of arbitrary high order, hence 00 in the limit. Moreover, the composition of the coordinate changes converges (in the 𝔪\mathfrak{m}-adic topology) to a formal coordinate change such that the residual part g⁡(xk+1,…,xn)g(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n}) in the theorem is a formal power series.

It remains to prove that if ff has an isolated singularity, then

f​∼ra1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g⁡(xk+1,…,xn)f\ \rsim\ a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n})

with ai∈K,ai≠0a_{i}\in K,a_{i}\neq 0, and g∈𝔪3∩K⁡⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩g\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}\cap K\langle x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle. This is a consequence of the following Theorem 2.2 since ff is right equivalent to a polynomial by Corollary 1.7 (hence an algebraic power series) and the fact that algebraic power series are convergent (Lemma 1.4). ∎

We prove now the splitting lemma for the ring of algebraic power series K​⟨𝒙⟩a​l​gK\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle^{alg}. We call a KK-algebra automorphism of K​⟨𝒙⟩a​l​gK\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle^{alg} an algebraic coordinate change.

Theorem 2.2 (Algebraic splitting lemma in characteristic ≠2\neq 2).

Let KK be any field and f∈𝔪2f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2} be an algebraic power series with rank⁡H⁡(f)=k\rank H(f)=k. Then

f​∼ra1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g⁡(xk+1,…,xn),f\ \rsim\ a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n}),

with ai∈K,ai≠0a_{i}\in K,a_{i}\neq 0. The right equivalence is given by an algebraic coordinate change, and the residual part g∈𝔪3g\in\mathfrak{m}^{3} is an algebraic power series. gg is uniquely determined up to right equivalence in K​⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩a​l​gK\langle x_{k+1},...,x_{n}\rangle^{alg}.

Proof.

Theorem 2.1 implies that

f⁡(φ¯1​(x),…,φ¯n​(x))=a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g¯​(xk+1,…,xn)f(\bar{\varphi}_{1}(x),\ldots,\bar{\varphi}_{n}(x))=a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+\bar{g}(x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n})

for a suitable g¯∈K⁡[[xk+1,…,xn]]\bar{g}\in K[[x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n}]] of order ≥3\geq 3, and an automorphism φ¯=(φ¯1​(x),…,φ¯n​(x))\bar{\varphi}=(\bar{\varphi}_{1}(x),\ldots,\bar{\varphi}_{n}(x)) of K⁡[[x]]K[[x]]. From Theorem 5 we deduce the existence of φ⁡(x)=(φ1​(x),…,φn​(x))∈(K​⟨𝒙⟩a​l​g)n\varphi(x)=(\varphi_{1}(x),\ldots,\varphi_{n}(x))\in(K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle^{alg})^{n} and g⁡(xk+1,…,xn)∈K​⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩a​l​gg(x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n})\in K\langle x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg} such that

f⁡(φ1​(x),…,φn​(x))=a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g⁡(xk+1,…,xn)f(\varphi_{1}(x),\ldots,\varphi_{n}(x))=a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g(x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n})

and

φ¯≡φ​ mod ​𝔪4,g¯≡g​ mod ​𝔪4.\bar{\varphi}\equiv\varphi\text{ mod }\mathfrak{m}^{4},\bar{g}\equiv g\text{ mod }\mathfrak{m}^{4}.

This implies that φ\varphi is an automorphism of K​⟨𝒙⟩a​l​gK\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle^{alg} and g∈𝔪3g\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}.
Now assume that

a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g1​(xk+1,…,xn)∼a1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g2​(xk+1,…,xn)a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g_{1}(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n})\sim a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g_{2}(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n})

for g1,g2∈K​⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩a​l​gg_{1},g_{2}\in K\langle x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg}. Theorem 2.1 implies that g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are right equivalent in K⁡[[xk+1,…,xn]]K[[x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n}]]. Theorem 5 implies that they are also right equivalent in K​⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩a​l​gK\langle x_{k+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg}. ∎

Corollary 2.3.

Let KK be an arbitrary field of characteristic ≠2\neq 2 and K​⟨𝐱⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle be either K⁡[[𝐱]]K[[\boldsymbol{x}]] or K​⟨𝐱⟩a​l​gK\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle^{alg} and f∈𝔪2f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}. Assume moreover that KK coincides with its subfield K2K^{2} of squares. Then

f​∼rx12+…+xk2+g⁡(xk+1,…,xn),f\ \rsim x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+x_{k}^{2}+g(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n}),

with gg uniquely determined up to right equivalence. The same holds for f∈K​⟨𝐱⟩f\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle, with KK a real valued field, provided ff has an isolated singularity.

Proof.

If K2=KK^{2}=K, then ai∈K\sqrt{a_{i}}\in K (this is the only condition we need) and the quadratic form a1​x12+…+ak​xk2a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2} is equivalent to x12+…+xk2x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+x_{k}^{2}. The result follows from Theorems 2.1 and 2.2. ∎

We are now going to prove the splitting lemma in the analytic case. An element ff in K​⟨𝒙⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle, K∈{ℂ,ℝ}K\in\{{\mathbb{C}},{\mathbb{R}}\} with absolute value as valuation, is called an analytic power series and an automorphism of K​⟨𝒙⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle an analytic coordinate change.

Theorem 2.4 (Analytic splitting lemma).

Let KK be either ℂ{\mathbb{C}} or ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and K​⟨𝐱⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle the usual convergent power series ring. Let f∈𝔪2⊂K​⟨𝐱⟩f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}\subset K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle with rank⁡H⁡(f)=k\rank H(f)=k. Then

f​∼ra1​x12+…+ak​xk2+g⁡(xk+1,…,xn),f\ \rsim\ a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2}+g(x_{k+1},\dots,x_{n}),

given by an analytic coordinate change, with ai=1a_{i}=1 if K=ℂK={\mathbb{C}} and ai±1a_{i}\pm 1 if K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}}, and g∈𝔪3g\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}. The residual part gg is an analytic power series that is uniquely determined up to right equivalence in K⁡⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩K\langle x_{k+1},...,x_{n}\rangle.

We do not require that ff hs an isolated singularity. For the proof we need the notion of (versal) unfoldings, which can be formulated for any real valued field KK.

Definition 2.5.

Let f∈𝔪⊂K⁡⟨𝐱⟩=K⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩f\in\mathfrak{m}\subset K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle=K\langle x_{1},...,x_{n}\rangle.

  1. 1.

    An (r-parameter) unfolding of ff is a power series F∈K​⟨𝒙,𝒖⟩F\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u}\rangle, 𝒖=(u1,…,ur)\boldsymbol{u}=(u_{1},...,u_{r}), such that F⁡(𝒙,𝟎)=fF(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{0})=f.
    If F⁡(𝒙,𝒖)=f⁡(𝒙)F(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u})=f(\boldsymbol{x}) we say that FF is the constant unfolding of ff.

  2. 2.

    Let F∈K​⟨𝒙,𝒖⟩F\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u}\rangle and G∈K​⟨𝒙,𝒗⟩G\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{v}\rangle, 𝒗=(v1,…,vs)\boldsymbol{v}=(v_{1},...,v_{s}), be two unfoldings of ff. A morphism from FF to GG is given by a pair

    (Φ,α):F→G,(\Phi,\alpha):F\to G,
    1. (i)

      Φ:K⁡⟨𝒙,𝒗⟩→K⁡⟨𝒙,𝒖⟩\Phi:K\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{v}\rangle\to K\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u}\rangle, a KK-algebra mormhism with
      Φ⁡(xi)=:φi∈K⁡⟨𝒙,𝒖⟩\Phi(x_{i})=:\varphi_{i}\in K\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u}\rangle, φi​(𝒙,𝟎)=xi\varphi_{i}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{0})=x_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,...,n,
      Φ⁡(vj)=:ϕj∈K⁡⟨𝒖⟩\Phi(v_{j})=:\phi_{j}\in K\langle\boldsymbol{u}\rangle, ϕj​(𝟎)=0\phi_{j}(\boldsymbol{0})=0, j=1,…,s\ j=1,...,s, and

    2. (ii)

      α∈K​⟨𝒖⟩\alpha\in K\langle\boldsymbol{u}\rangle, α⁡(𝟎)=0\alpha(\boldsymbol{0})=0,

    such that F⁡(𝒙,𝒖)=Φ⁡(G)​(𝒙,𝒖)+α⁡(𝒖)F(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u})=\Phi(G)(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u})+\alpha(\boldsymbol{u}).

    If this holds, we say that FF is induced from GG by Φ\Phi. If Φ\Phi is an isomorphism (which implies r=sr=s), we say that FF and GG are isomorphic unfoldings.

  3. 3.

    An unfolding FF of ff is called versal (or complete in the terminology of [GLS07]) if any unfolding of ff is induced from FF by a suitable morphism. A versal unfolding FF with minimal number of parameters rr is called miniversal.

The following theorem is due to J. Mather for C∞C^{\infty}-functions.

Theorem 2.6.

Let KK be ℝ{\mathbb{R}} or ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with the usual real valuations and f∈𝔪⊂K​⟨𝐱⟩f\in\mathfrak{m}\subset K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle.

  1. 1.

    The singularity ff has a versal unfolding if and only if μ⁡(f)\mu(f) is finite.

  2. 2.

    Two rr-parameter versal unfoldings of ff are isomorphic.

  3. 3.

    Every versal unfolding of ff is isomorphic to a constant unfolding of a miniversal unfolding of ff.

  4. 4.

    If {b1,…,br}⊂𝔪\{b_{1},...,b_{r}\}\subset\mathfrak{m} represents a KK-basis of 𝔪/⟨∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xn⟩\mathfrak{m}/\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}},...,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\rangle, then

    F⁡(𝒙,𝒖)=f⁡(𝒙)+u1​b1​(𝒙)+…+ur​br​(𝒙)F(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{u})=f(\boldsymbol{x})+u_{1}b_{1}(\boldsymbol{x})+...+u_{r}b_{r}(\boldsymbol{x})

    is a miniversal unfolding of ff.

Proof.

For a proof in the C∞C^{\infty}-case see [Br75]. It uses the existence and uniqueness of the solution of an ODE (together with the smooth dependence of the initial conditions) to prove an infinitesimal characterization of local triviality (similar to that in [GLS07, Theorem 1.2.22]). The theorem holds thus for the real and complex analytic case as well. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.4.

As in the formal case we can assume that f⁡(𝒙)=q+gf(\boldsymbol{x})=q+g, where

q⁡(x1,…,xk)=a1​x12+…+ak​xk2,ai∈K∖{0},q(x_{1},...,x_{k})=a_{1}x_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{k}x_{k}^{2},\ a_{i}\in K\smallsetminus\{0\},

(in fact, ai=1a_{i}=1 if K=ℂK={\mathbb{C}} and ai=±1a_{i}=\pm 1 if K=ℝK={\mathbb{R}}) and g⁡(x1,…,xn)∈𝔪3g(x_{1},...,x_{n})\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}. Setting g′​(x1,…,xk):=g⁡(x1,…,xk,0,…,0)g^{\prime}(x_{1},...,x_{k}):=g(x_{1},...,x_{k},0,...,0) we get g⁡(x1,…,xn)=g′​(x1,…,xk)+h⁡(x1,…,xn)g(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=g^{\prime}(x_{1},...,x_{k})+h(x_{1},...,x_{n}), with h=∑i=k+1nxi​hi​(x1,…,xn)h=\sum_{i=k+1}^{n}x_{i}h_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{n}). Then f=f′+h,f=f^{\prime}+h, h∈𝔪3h\in\mathfrak{m}^{3},

f′​(x1,…,xk):=f⁡(x1,…,xk,0,…,0)=q⁡(x1,…,xk)+g′​(x1,…,xk).f^{\prime}(x_{1},...,x_{k}):=f(x_{1},...,x_{k},0,...,0)=q(x_{1},...,x_{k})+g^{\prime}(x_{1},...,x_{k}).

qq has Milnor number 1 and hence is 2-determined by Corollary 1.7. Since g′∈𝔪3g^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}, it follows that f′f^{\prime} is right equivalent to qq by an automorphism φ\varphi of K⁡⟨x1,…,xk⟩K\langle x_{1},...,x_{k}\rangle. Setting φi​(x1,…,xk):=φ⁡(xi)\varphi_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{k}):=\varphi(x_{i}), we have

φ⁡(f′)=q⁡(φ1,…,φk)+g′​(φ1,…,φk)=q⁡(x1,…,xk).\varphi(f^{\prime})=q(\varphi_{1},...,\varphi_{k})+g^{\prime}(\varphi_{1},...,\varphi_{k})=q(x_{1},...,x_{k}).

Now define the automorphism ψ\psi of K⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩K\langle x_{1},...,x_{n}\rangle by xi↦φi​(x1,…,xk)x_{i}\mapsto\varphi_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{k}) for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k, and xi↦xix_{i}\mapsto x_{i} for i>ki>k. Then ψ⁡(f′)=φ⁡(f′)=q\psi(f^{\prime})=\varphi(f^{\prime})=q and we have

ψ⁡(f)=ψ⁡(f′)+ψ⁡(h)=q+∑i=k+1nxi​hi​(φ1,…,φk,xk+1,…,xn).\psi(f)=\psi(f^{\prime})+\psi(h)=q+\sum_{i=k+1}^{n}x_{i}h_{i}(\varphi_{1},...,\varphi_{k},x_{k+1},...,x_{n}).

Thus, after applying ψ\psi, we may assume that f=q+hf=q+h, h=∑i=k+1nxi​hi​(x1,…,xn).h=\sum_{i=k+1}^{n}x_{i}h_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{n}). That is f⁡(x1,…,xk,0,…,0)=qf(x_{1},...,x_{k},0,...,0)=q, in other words, ff is an unfolding of qq.

Since ⟨∂q∂x1,…,∂q∂xk⟩=⟨x1,…,xk⟩\langle\frac{\partial q}{\partial x_{1}},...,\frac{\partial q}{\partial x_{k}}\rangle=\langle x_{1},...,x_{k}\rangle, qq is a miniversal unfolding of itself by Theorem 2.6 and ff is isomorphic to the (n−r)(n-r)-paramter constant unfolding of qq. Hence this constant unfolding of qq can be induced from ff by an isomorphism (Φ,α)(\Phi,\alpha) from qq to ff. By Definition 2.5 this means that Φ\Phi is an automorphism of K⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩K\langle x_{1},...,x_{n}\rangle, Φ⁡(xi)​(x1,…,xk,0,…,0)=xi\Phi(x_{i})(x_{1},...,x_{k},0,...,0)=x_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,...,k, and Φ⁡(xi)∈K⁡⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩,Φ⁡(0)=0\Phi(x_{i})\in K\langle x_{k+1},...,x_{n}\rangle,\Phi(0)=0, for i=k+1,…,ni=k+1,...,n such that q=Φ⁡(f)+α⁡(xk+1,…,xn).q=\Phi(f)+\alpha(x_{k+1},...,x_{n}). The uniqueness of g=−αg=-\alpha follows from Theorem 2.1. This proves the theorem. ∎

3 Splitting Lemma in Characteristic 2

In this section let KK be a field of characteristic 2. We have the following classification of quadratic forms in characteristic 2, due to C. Arf in [Ar41, Satz 2].

Theorem 3.1.

Let f=∑1≤i≤j≤nai​j​xi​xj∈K⁡[x1,…,xn]f=\sum_{1\leq i\leq j\leq n}a_{ij}x_{i}x_{j}\in K[x_{1},...,x_{n}] be a quadratic form. Then ff is equivalent to the following normal form:

∑i​ odd, ​i=12​l−1(ai​xi2+xi​xi+1+ai+1​xi+12)+∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2,\sum_{i\text{ odd, }i=1}^{2l-1}(a_{i}x_{i}^{2}+x_{i}x_{i+1}+a_{i+1}x_{i+1}^{2})+\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2},

with ai,di∈Ka_{i},d_{i}\in K. Moreover, the form ∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2} is uniquely determined by ff up to linear coordinate change. The first sum is not unique but 2​l2l, the rank of H⁡(f)H(f), is.

Proof.

Arf proves in [Ar41, Satz 2] that ff is equivalent to

∑i​ odd, ​i=12​l−1(ai​xi2+bi​xi​xi+1+ci+1​xi+12)+∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2,\sum_{i\text{ odd, }i=1}^{2l-1}(a_{i}x_{i}^{2}+b_{i}x_{i}x_{i+1}+c_{i+1}x_{i+1}^{2})+\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2},

with ai,bi,ci,di∈Ka_{i},b_{i},c_{i},d_{i}\in K, bi≠0b_{i}\neq 0, together with the uniqueness statements. By setting xi↦1bi​xix_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{b_{i}}x_{i} for ii odd, i=1,…,2​l−1i=1,...,2l-1, and calling aibi2\frac{a_{i}}{b_{i}^{2}} again aia_{i}, we get the required form. ∎

Corollary 3.2.

Assume moreover that quadratic equations are solvable in KK. Then ff is equivalent to one of the following normal forms:

(a)x1​x2+x3​x4+…+x2​l−1​x2​l+x2​l+12,1≤2​l+1≤n,(b)x1​x2+x3​x4+…+x2​l−1​x2​l,2≤2​l≤n.\begin{array}[]{llll}(a)&x_{1}x_{2}+x_{3}x_{4}+\ldots+x_{2l-1}x_{2l}+x_{2l+1}^{2},&1\leq 2l+1\leq n,\\ (b)&x_{1}x_{2}+x_{3}x_{4}+\ldots+x_{2l-1}x_{2l},&2\leq 2l\leq n.\end{array}
Proof.

For each ii odd, i=1,…,2​l−1i=1,...,2l-1, we make the following transformations:
First xi↦xi+u​xi+1x_{i}\mapsto x_{i}+ux_{i+1} where uu is a solution of ai​u2+u+ai+1=0a_{i}u^{2}+u+a_{i+1}=0, and then apply xi+1↦xi+1+ai​xix_{i+1}\mapsto x_{i+1}+a_{i}x_{i} .
This transforms ai​xi2+xi​xi+1+ai+1​xi+12↦xi​xi+1a_{i}x_{i}^{2}+x_{i}x_{i+1}+a_{i+1}x_{i+1}^{2}\mapsto x_{i}x_{i+1}. Moreover, let (after renumbering) di≠0d_{i}\neq 0 for i=2​l+1,…,2​l+k,k≥0i=2l+1,...,2l+k,\ k\geq 0, and 0 else. Setting now xi↦1di​xix_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{i}}}x_{i}, if 2​l+1≤i≤2​l+k2l+1\leq i\leq 2l+k, we get for the last sum x2​l+12+…+x2​l+k2=(x2​l+1+…+x2​l+k)2x_{2l+1}^{2}+...+x_{2l+k}^{2}=(x_{2l+1}+...+x_{2l+k})^{2} with k≥0k\geq 0. We get the normal form (b) if k=0k=0. If k≥1k\geq 1 we set x2​l+1=x2​l+1+…+x2​l+kx_{2l+1}=x_{2l+1}+...+x_{2l+k} and get form (a). ∎

Remark 3.3.

Given a quadratic form f=∑1≤i≤j≤nai​j​xi​xj∈K⁡[x1,…,xn]f=\sum_{1\leq i\leq j\leq n}a_{ij}x_{i}x_{j}\in K[x_{1},...,x_{n}], Arf introduces in [Ar41] the vector space V=K​v1+…+K​vnV=Kv_{1}+...+Kv_{n} with a metric defined by the bilinear form v⋅w=f⁡(v+w)−f⁡(v)−f⁡(w)=∑1≤i<j≤nai​j​(xi​yj+xj​yi)v\cdot w=f(v+w)-f(v)-f(w)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}a_{ij}(x_{i}y_{j}+x_{j}y_{i}) for the two vectors v=∑ixi​viv=\sum_{i}x_{i}v_{i} and w=∑iyi​viw=\sum_{i}y_{i}v_{i}. He proves then that VV decomposes as an orthogonal sum V′⊕V∗V^{\prime}\oplus V^{*} with V∗={w∣w⋅v=0​∀v∈V}V^{*}=\{w\mid w\cdot v=0\,\,\forall\,v\in V\} the subspace of vectors that are orthogonal to all vectors of VV. V∗V^{*} decomposes as an orthogonal sum of 1-dimensional subspaces, V∗=⊕i=2​l+1n⟨vi⟩V^{*}=\oplus_{i=2l+1}^{n}\langle v_{i}\rangle and V′V^{\prime} is the direct sum of 2-dimensional subspaces, V′=⊕i​ odd, ​i=12​l−1⟨vi,vi+1⟩V^{\prime}=\oplus_{i\text{ odd, }i=1}^{2l-1}\langle v_{i},v_{i+1}\rangle with vi⋅vi+1≠0v_{i}\cdot v_{i+1}\neq 0. Since φ⁡(v⋅w)=φ⁡(v)​φ​(w)\varphi(v\cdot w)=\varphi(v)\varphi(w) it follows that V∗V^{*} is invariant under any linear coordinate change φ\varphi, while V′V^{\prime} is a non-invariant complement of V∗V^{*} of even dimension. This proves the normal form of ff in Theorem 3.1 and that the form ∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2} is unique up to equivalence.

Lemma 3.4.

Let KK be any field. The power series

f=∑i​ odd, ​i=12​l−1(ai​xi2+bi​xi​xi+1+ai+1​xi+12)+∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2+h⁡(x1,…,xn),f=\sum_{i\text{ odd, }i=1}^{2l-1}(a_{i}x_{i}^{2}+b_{i}x_{i}x_{i+1}+a_{i+1}x_{i+1}^{2})+\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2}+h(x_{1},...,x_{n}),

Proof.

Write h=f3+x1​g1+…+x2​l​g2​lh=f_{3}+x_{1}g_{1}+...+x_{2l}g_{2l} with gi​(x1,…,xn)∈𝔪2g_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{n})\in\mathfrak{m}^{2} and f3∈𝔪3f_{3}\in\mathfrak{m}^{3} not depending on x1,…,x2​lx_{1},...,x_{2l}. The coordinate change

transforms ff to

Comparing the quadratic terms of (* ‣ 3), we get

ℓ:=l1​l2+…+l2​l−1​l2​l+a​x2​l+12=x1​x2+…+x2​l−1​x2​l+a​x2​l+12,\ell:=l_{1}l_{2}+\ldots+l_{2l-1}l_{2l}+\ ax_{2l+1}^{2}=x_{1}x_{2}+\ldots+x_{2l-1}x_{2l}+\ ax_{2l+1}^{2},

and ∂ℓ∂xi=xi+1\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial x_{i}}=x_{i+1} if ii is odd and ∂ℓ∂xi=xi−1\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial x_{i}}=x_{i-1} if ii is even for i≤2​li\leq 2l. Since ∂ℓ∂xi∈⟨l1,…,l2​l⟩\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial x_{i}}\in\langle l_{1},...,l_{2l}\rangle, it follows that ⟨x1,…,x2​l⟩⊂⟨l1,…,l2​l⟩\langle x_{1},...,x_{2l}\rangle\subset\langle l_{1},...,l_{2l}\rangle and hence, with li′​(x1,…,x2​l):=li​(x1,…,x2​l,0,…,0)l^{\prime}_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{2l}):=l_{i}(x_{1},...,x_{2l},0,...,0), we get ⟨x1,…,x2​l⟩=⟨l1′,…,l2​l′⟩\langle x_{1},...,x_{2l}\rangle=\langle l^{\prime}_{1},...,l^{\prime}_{2l}\rangle. Hence det(∂li∂xj)i,j=1,…,2​l=det(∂li′∂xj)i,j=1,…,2​l≠0\det\big(\frac{\partial l_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\big)_{i,j=1,...,2l}=\det\big(\frac{\partial l^{\prime}_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\big)_{i,j=1,...,2l}\neq 0.

To proove 2.(a) note that if ff has an isolated singularity then ff is right equivalent (by a convergent coordinate change) to a polynomial, which is an algebraic powers series. This reduces the case to 2.(b).

To prove 2.(b) we use 1. and get

f⁡(φ¯)=∑i​ odd, ​i=12​l−1(ai​xi2+xi​xi+1+ai+1​xi+12)+∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2+h¯​(x2​l+1,…,xn),f(\bar{\varphi})=\sum_{i\text{ odd, }i=1}^{2l-1}(a_{i}x_{i}^{2}+x_{i}x_{i+1}+a_{i+1}x_{i+1}^{2})+\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2}+\bar{h}(x_{2l+1},...,x_{n}),

with φ¯=(φ¯1,…,φ¯n)\bar{\varphi}=(\bar{\varphi}_{1},\ldots,\bar{\varphi}_{n}) an automorphism of K⁡[[x1,…,xn]]K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]] and h¯∈𝔪3∩K⁡[[xl+1,…,xn]]\bar{h}\in\mathfrak{m}^{3}\cap K[[x_{l+1},\ldots,x_{n}]]. Theorem 5 implies the existence of φ∈(K​⟨x1,…,xn⟩a​l​g)n\varphi\in(K\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg})^{n} and h∈K​⟨xl+1,…,xn⟩a​l​gh\in K\langle x_{l+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg} such that

f⁡(φ)=∑i​ odd, ​i=12​l−1(ai​xi2+xi​xi+1+ai+1​xi+12)+∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2+h⁡(x2​l+1,…,xn)f(\varphi)=\sum_{i\text{ odd, }i=1}^{2l-1}(a_{i}x_{i}^{2}+x_{i}x_{i+1}+a_{i+1}x_{i+1}^{2})+\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2}+h(x_{2l+1},...,x_{n})

and

φ¯≡φ​ mod ​𝔪4​ and ​h¯≡h​ mod ​𝔪4.\bar{\varphi}\equiv\varphi\text{ mod }\mathfrak{m}^{4}\text{ and }\bar{h}\equiv h\text{ mod }\mathfrak{m}^{4}.

This implies that h∈𝔪3h\in\mathfrak{m}^{3} and φ\varphi defines an automorphism of K​⟨x1,…,xn⟩a​l​gK\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg}. Now assume given fj=∑i​ odd, ​i=12​l−1(ai​xi2+xi​xi+1+ai+1​xi+12)+∑i=2​l+1ndi​xi2+hj​(x2​l+1,…,xn)f_{j}=\sum_{i\text{ odd, }i=1}^{2l-1}(a_{i}x_{i}^{2}+x_{i}x_{i+1}+a_{i+1}x_{i+1}^{2})+\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2}+h_{j}(x_{2l+1},...,x_{n}), j=1,2j=1,2 such that f1∼f2f_{1}\sim f_{2} in K​⟨x1,…,xn⟩a​l​gK\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg}. The first part of the Theorem implies that h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} are right equivalent in K⁡[[xl+1,…,xn]]K[[x_{l+1},\ldots,x_{n}]]. From Theorem 5 we deduce that they are also right equivalent in K​⟨xl+1,…,xn⟩a​l​gK\langle x_{l+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{alg}. ∎

Remark 3.6.

As in Theorem 2.1, the uniqueness of the residual part gg does not only hold for K⁡[[𝐱]]K[[\boldsymbol{x}]] but for general K​⟨𝐱⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle, KK a real valued field:
Let f0,f1∈𝔪2⊂K⁡⟨𝐱⟩f_{0},f_{1}\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}\subset K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle and assume that

f0=q⁡(x1,…,x2​l)+g0​(x2​l+1,…,xn)​∼rf1=q⁡(x1,…,x2​l)+g1​(x2​l+1,…,xn)f_{0}=q(x_{1},...,x_{2l})+g_{0}(x_{2l+1},\dots,x_{n})\rsim f_{1}=q(x_{1},...,x_{2l})+g_{1}(x_{2l+1},\dots,x_{n})

with

and

gj=∑i=2​l+1ndixi2+hj,hj∈⟨x2​l+1,…,xn⟩3,di≠0,j=0,1.g_{j}=\sum_{i=2l+1}^{n}d_{i}x_{i}^{2}+h_{j},\ h_{j}\in\langle x_{2l+1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle^{3},\ d_{i}\neq 0,\ j=0,1.

Then g0​∼rg1g_{0}\rsim g_{1} in K⁡⟨xk+1,…,xn⟩K\langle x_{k+1},...,x_{n}\rangle.

This follows because we use in the proof of Theorem 2.1 (1) only the implicit function theorem, which holds for K​⟨𝐱⟩K\langle\boldsymbol{x}\rangle.

Together with Corollary 3.2 we get from Theorem 3.5:

Corollary 3.7.

Assume moreover that quadratic equations are solvable in KK. Then there exists an ll, 0≤2​l≤n0\leq 2l\leq n, such that f∈𝔪2⊂K⁡[[𝐱]]f\in\mathfrak{m}^{2}\subset K[[\boldsymbol{x}]] is right equivalent to one of the normal forms, with gg unique up to right equivalence:

(a)x1​x2+x3​x4+…+x2​l−1​x2​l+x2​l+12+g⁡(x2​l+1,…,xn),1≤2​l+1≤n,(b)x1​x2+x3​x4+…+x2​l−1​x2​l+g⁡(x2​l+1,…,xn),2≤2​l≤n.\begin{array}[]{llll}(a)&x_{1}x_{2}+x_{3}x_{4}+\ldots+x_{2l-1}x_{2l}+x_{2l+1}^{2}&+g(x_{2l+1},\ldots,x_{n}),&1\leq 2l+1\leq n,\\ (b)&x_{1}x_{2}+x_{3}x_{4}+\ldots+x_{2l-1}x_{2l}&+g(x_{2l+1},\ldots,x_{n}),&2\leq 2l\leq n.\end{array}

Moreover, statement 2. of Theorem 3.5 holds analogously.
